passages.t: ‘Enter His gates with thanksgiving’: a song for coming in
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A Psalm of thanksgiving” (verse 1). It is only five verses long, and almost every line is a command to praise.

“Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth” (verse 1). “Serve the LORD with gladness; come into His presence with joyful songs” (verse 2).

The middle verse gives the reason. “Know that the LORD is God. It is He who made us, and we are His; we are His people, and the sheep of His pasture” (verse 3).

Then come more commands, as if the worshippers are walking closer. “Enter His gates with thanksgiving and His courts with praise; give thanks to Him and bless His name” (verse 4).

And the last verse gives the reason again, in three short lines. “For the LORD is good, and His loving devotion endures forever; His faithfulness continues to all generations” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The Hebrew word in the heading is todah. It can mean thanks in general, or the thank offering, a sacrifice brought to the temple to give thanks for a rescue (Leviticus 7:12). Some scholars think this psalm was sung as people carried that offering through the temple gates. Others take the heading more simply, as a label for a song of praise.

The temple had gates and then courts, each one closer to the holy place. To enter ‘His gates’ and then ‘His courts’ was a real walk, step by step, singing.

‘Serve’ in verse 2 is the word for a servant's work and also for worship. A people served its king with labour and taxes. This people serves its King with gladness.

There is a small puzzle in verse 3. The Hebrew can be read two ways, because two words sound the same but are spelled differently. The written text says, ‘It is He who made us, and not we ourselves.’ The reading noted in the margin of the Hebrew Bible says, ‘It is He who made us, and we are His.’ Older English Bibles, like the King James, followed the first. Most modern Bibles, like the one on this site, follow the second. Ancient translations are divided too. Both readings say something true: we did not make ourselves, and we belong to the one who did.
passages.later:
Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd. I know My sheep and My sheep know Me” (John 10:14). Paul wrote, “we are God's workmanship” (Ephesians 2:10), and, “Give thanks in every circumstance, for this is God's will for you in Christ Jesus” (1 Thessalonians 5:18).

Paul also used the language of temple service for daily life: “offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God” (Romans 12:1).
passages.asks:
How do you come into God's presence? Psalm 100 suggests a simple door: thanks. Before you ask for anything, thank God for one thing he has done. Then another.

And let verse 3 settle something deep. You did not make yourself. You belong to someone, and he is good. That is a reason for gladness on a hard day as much as on an easy one.
